2.1 The ionic model 
Structure of ionic compounds 
In solid ionic compounds, the ions are held in fixed positions by strong 
electrostatic forces of attraction, so these compounds have high melting 
points and very low electrical conductivity. In contrast, molten ionic 
compounds are good electrical conductors because their ions are able to 
move and act as charge carriers. These mobile ions are still held together by 
strong electrostatic forces, so ionic compounds have low volatility and high 
boiling points. Most icnic solids are soluble in polar solvents such as water, but 
insoluble in non-polar solvents such as hexane.

Experimental lattice enthalpies cannot be determined directly, but they 
can be deduced from Born-Haber cycles (Reactivity 1.2 AHL). Theoretical 
lattice enthalpies can be calculated, assuming that the ions are perfect 
spheres and the bonding is 100% ionic. 
Any differences between the experimental and theoretical lattice enthalpy 
values suggest that the bonding between the ions has a degree of covalent 
character (Structure 2.2). This is commonly encountered in compounds 
with large anions, which cannot hold their valence electrons tightly 
and partially share their electron clouds with neighbouring cations. The

In the solid state, the ions are held in fixed positions by ionic bonding, so they cannot move and therefore cannot carry electric charge. In the liquid (molten) state, the ions can move and it is the ions that act as charge carriers.
To separate an ionic lattice into individual ions, strong ionic bonds must be broken. This process requires energy, which can be compensated by forming ion–dipole and, in some cases, hydrogen bonds between the ions and solvent molecules. Such bonds can be formed only by polar solvents, such as water. Non-polar solvents can interact with ions only by weak London dispersion forces, the energy of which is insufficient for breaking the ionic lattice.
